Soon we heard him call down.

“How much farther do I have to go?”

“How high are you?” Legrand asked.

“A very long way,” the Black man answered. “I can see the sky through the treetop.”

“Forget the sky and listen to me. Look down the trunk and count the branches beneath you on this side. How many have you passed?”

“One, two, three, four, five. I’ve passed five big branches on this side, master.”

“Then climb one branch higher.”

A few minutes later, his voice announced that he had reached the seventh branch.

“Now, Jup,” Legrand called, plainly excited, “I want you to move along that branch as far as you can. Tell me if you notice anything unusual.” By now, whatever slight doubt I still had about my poor friend’s madness had disappeared. I could only conclude that he had lost his mind, and I grew seriously worried about getting him home. While I considered what to do, Jupiter spoke again.

“I’m almost afraid to go far out on this branch. It’s dead nearly all the way along.”

“Did you say the branch was dead, Jupiter?” Legrand asked, his voice shaking.

“Yes, master, dead as a doornail. Finished for certain. Departed this life.”

“What in heaven’s name am I to do?” Legrand asked, apparently in great distress.

“Do?” I said, glad of a chance to speak. “Come home and go to bed. Come along, be sensible! It’s getting late, and remember your promise.”

“Jupiter,” he called, completely ignoring me, “can you hear me?”

“Yes, Master Will, perfectly clearly.”

“Then test the wood carefully with your knife. See whether you think it’s badly rotten.”

“It’s certainly rotten, master,” the Black man replied after a few moments, “but it could be worse. I might risk going a little way out by myself.”

“By yourself? What do you mean?”

“I mean the bug. It’s a very heavy bug. Suppose I drop it first. Then the branch won’t break under the weight of just one Black man.”

“You damned scoundrel!” Legrand cried, looking much relieved. “What do you mean by telling me such nonsense? Drop that beetle and I’ll break your neck. Listen, Jupiter. Do you hear me?”

“Yes, master. You don’t need to shout at a poor Black man like that.”

“Well, listen carefully. If you go as far along the branch as you think is safe, without dropping the beetle, I’ll give you a silver dollar as soon as you come down.”

He was short but stood remarkably straight, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He opened his lecture with a review of chemistry’s history and the advances made by different scholars, speaking the names of its greatest discoverers with enthusiasm. Then he briefly described the science as it stood today and explained many basic terms. After a few introductory experiments, he ended with praise of modern chemistry that I will never forget:

“Those who taught this science long ago,” he said, “promised impossible things and accomplished nothing. Today’s masters promise very little. They know that one metal cannot be changed into another and that a potion granting eternal life is a fantasy. Yet these thinkers, whose hands seem fit only for dirty work and whose eyes seem made to stare into microscopes or melting pots, have performed miracles. They enter nature’s hidden places and reveal how she works. They rise into the heavens. They have discovered how blood circulates and what the air we breathe is made of. They have gained new and almost limitless powers. They can command thunder from the sky, imitate earthquakes, and even challenge the invisible world with images of its own shadows.”

These were the professor’s words—or, rather, the words of fate, spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were wrestling with a real enemy. One by one, he touched the keys that controlled my being, sounding chord after chord until a single thought, a single idea, a single purpose filled my mind. So much has already been achieved, Frankenstein’s soul cried, but I will achieve more, far more. Following the paths others have marked, I will discover a new way, investigate unknown powers, and reveal creation’s deepest mysteries to the world.

I did not sleep that night. My whole inner life was in revolt and confusion. I sensed that order would emerge, but I could do nothing to bring it about. After dawn, sleep gradually came. When I woke, the previous night’s thoughts seemed like a dream. Only my determination remained: I would return to my earlier studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private he was even gentler and more engaging than in public. During the lecture he had carried himself with a certain dignity; at home, this gave way to the warmest friendliness and kindness.

No imagination could capture the terrifying grandeur of such a spectacle occurring in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have provided a fitting comparison. Even in daylight my hair rose as I stared far down into the gaping depths, sending my imagination wandering through strange vaulted chambers, glowing gulfs, and dreadful red chasms of that hideous, bottomless fire. My escape had been narrow indeed. If the balloon had stayed in the cloud even a little longer—if getting wet had not irritated me enough to throw out the ballast—destruction would have been inevitable. Such dangers receive little attention, yet they may be the greatest hazards of balloon travel. By now, however, I had risen too high to worry about them further.

“I was climbing rapidly, and at seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of no less than nine and a half miles. Breathing became extremely difficult. My head also hurt terribly. After noticing moisture on my cheeks for some time, I finally realized it was blood flowing quite freely from my eardrums. My eyes caused me considerable discomfort too. When I passed a hand over them, they seemed to bulge far out of their sockets. Everything in the basket, and even the balloon itself, looked distorted. These symptoms were worse than I had expected and began to frighten me. At that moment, foolishly and without thinking, I threw three five-pound pieces of ballast from the basket. The resulting increase in speed carried me too quickly into a layer of very thin air, without allowing enough time to adjust. The consequences nearly destroyed both my expedition and me. A sudden spasm seized me and lasted more than five minutes. Even when it partly subsided, I could draw breath only in gasps separated by long intervals. All the while, blood poured from my nose and ears, with a little coming from my eyes as well. The pigeons looked desperately distressed and struggled to escape. The cat cried pitifully, her tongue hanging from her mouth, and staggered back and forth across the basket as though poisoned. Too late, I understood how recklessly I had acted in releasing the ballast. I became intensely agitated. I expected nothing less than death, and within a few minutes.
